paragraphs.paragraph: The psalm is designated a “Maschil” of David. Its opening verses ask why the mighty man boasts in mischief and affirm that the goodness of God endures continually.
paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Heading and Opening Question

easy.explanation: The heading identifies it as a Maschil of David.
easy.q: To whom is the Maschil attributed?

easy.explanation: The verse asks, “Why boastest thou thyself in mischief?”
easy.q: What does the mighty man boast in?

easy.explanation: The verse declares that the goodness of God endureth continually.

answers: A question about boasting in mischief
A question about building the temple
medium.explanation: The psalm opens by questioning the mighty man’s boasting in mischief.
medium.q: What kind of question opens the psalm?

answers: Human mischief and God’s enduring goodness
medium.explanation: The verse contrasts mischief with the continual goodness of God.
medium.q: What contrast appears in the opening verse?

medium.explanation: “Continually” emphasizes that God’s goodness endures without ceasing.

challenge.explanation: The question rebukes a person who takes pride in harmful or wicked behavior.
challenge.q: What moral problem is implied by the question, “Why boastest thou thyself in mischief”?

answers: From human boasting to God’s lasting goodness
From David’s wealth to Saul’s kingdom
challenge.explanation: The verse moves from the mighty man’s mischief to the enduring goodness of God.
challenge.q: How does the opening verse direct the reader’s attention?

answers: God’s goodness is presented as enduring
Both are described as equally lasting
challenge.explanation: The verse specifically says that God’s goodness endureth continually.
challenge.q: What does the opening suggest about the relative permanence of evil and goodness?

paragraphs.idea: The psalm is designated a “Maschil” of David. Its opening verses ask why the mighty man boasts in mischief and affirm that the goodness of God endures continually.

paragraphs.paragraph: The poet condemns the wicked man’s harmful speech and deceit. His tongue devises mischief like a sharp razor, and he loves evil and lying more than goodness and righteousness.
paragraphs.title: Condemnation of Evil Speech and Deceit

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs.”
The tongue is compared to “a sharp rasor.”
easy.q: What is the tongue compared to?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Thou lovest evil more than good.”
easy.q: What does the wicked man love more than good?

medium.explanation: A sharp razor suggests speech that can cut, wound, and destroy.
medium.q: What does the comparison to a sharp razor suggest about the tongue?

medium.explanation: The verse says he loves lying rather than speaking righteousness.
medium.q: What does the wicked man prefer to speaking righteousness?

medium.explanation: The tongue is described as “working deceitfully.”
medium.q: What kind of work does the tongue perform according to the passage?

answers: The wicked man prefers evil and lying to good and righteousness
The righteous prefer wealth to mercy
The mighty man prefers silence to speech
challenge.explanation: The passage presents a deliberate preference for evil and lying over goodness and righteousness.
challenge.q: What ethical reversal is described in these verses?

answers: It portrays speech as sharp and harmful
It portrays speech as soft and comforting
challenge.explanation: A razor can cut, making it an image of damaging and dangerous words.
challenge.q: Why is the razor image especially fitting for deceitful speech?

answers: His wrongdoing is presented as a chosen preference
His wrongdoing is shown as an accident
His wrongdoing is described as something he hates
challenge.explanation: The repeated statements that he loves evil and lying show a settled moral preference.
challenge.q: What does the repeated emphasis on love reveal about the wicked man?

paragraphs.idea: The poet condemns the wicked man’s harmful speech and deceit. His tongue devises mischief like a sharp razor, and he loves evil and lying more than goodness and righteousness.

paragraphs.paragraph: God will destroy and uproot the wicked man from his dwelling place and from the land of the living. The righteous will see, fear, and laugh at him because he trusted in riches and strengthened himself in wickedness instead of making God his strength.
paragraphs.title: The Punishment of the Wicked Informer

easy.explanation: The passage says God will destroy him and root him out of the land of the living.
easy.q: What will God do to the wicked man?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “The righteous also shall see, and fear.”
He trusted in the abundance of his riches.
easy.q: In what did the wicked man trust?

answers: A source of help and security
medium.explanation: Here, strength means a source of protection, help, and security.
medium.q: What does “strength” mean in the phrase “made not God his strength”?

answers: His false confidence will be exposed
They want to imitate his wickedness
They are afraid of his riches
medium.explanation: His trust in riches and wickedness will be shown to be vain.
medium.q: Why will the righteous laugh at the wicked man?

answers: He trusted riches and wickedness instead of God, so he is uprooted
He trusted God, so he was destroyed
He gave away his riches, so he was praised
medium.explanation: The passage connects his downfall with refusing to make God his strength.
medium.q: What is the connection between the wicked man’s trust and his punishment?

answers: The wicked trusts riches and wickedness, while God is the true strength
The wicked trusts God, while the righteous trust riches
The wicked praises righteousness, while the righteous praise deceit
challenge.explanation: The verses contrast misplaced human confidence with God as the true source of strength.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in these verses?

answers: Complete removal from earthly life and society
A temporary move to another house
challenge.explanation: The phrase portrays complete removal from the living community.
challenge.q: What does being rooted out of “the land of the living” communicate?

answers: They fear God’s judgment but mock the wicked man’s failed confidence
They fear the wicked man and desire his riches
They laugh because judgment has disappeared
challenge.explanation: The righteous respond with awe at judgment and derision toward the wicked man’s ruin.
challenge.q: Why are both fear and laughter attributed to the righteous?

paragraphs.idea: God will destroy and uproot the wicked man from his dwelling place and from the land of the living. The righteous will see, fear, and laugh at him because he trusted in riches and strengthened himself in wickedness instead of making God his strength.

paragraphs.paragraph: In contrast to the wicked man, the poet is like a green olive tree in the house of God. He trusts in God’s mercy forever, praises God because of what He has done, and waits on His good name before the saints.
paragraphs.title: The Poet’s Trust and Thanksgiving

easy.explanation: He says, “I am like a green olive tree in the house of God.”
easy.q: What is the poet compared to?

easy.explanation: The poet says, “I trust in the mercy of God.”
easy.q: In what does the poet trust?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it.”
easy.q: Why will the poet praise God?

answers: Removal from the land of the living
medium.explanation: A green olive tree suggests vitality and flourishing in God’s house.
medium.q: What does the image of a green olive tree suggest?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever.”
medium.q: How long does the poet say he will trust in God’s mercy?

medium.explanation: The poet waits on God’s name because it is good before His saints.
medium.q: Before whom is God’s name described as good?

answers: He trusts God’s mercy and flourishes, rather than trusting riches and wickedness
He boasts in evil more than the wicked man
He is uprooted from the land of the living
challenge.explanation: The poet’s trust in God’s mercy contrasts with the wicked man’s trust in riches and evil.
challenge.q: How does the poet contrast himself with the wicked man?

answers: Trust in God’s mercy leads the poet to continual praise
Trust in riches leads the poet to righteousness
Fear of the saints leads the poet to deceit
challenge.explanation: Because he trusts God’s mercy, the poet promises to praise Him forever.
challenge.q: What relationship between trust and praise appears in these verses?

answers: It is intended to be continual
It is limited to one occasion
It is offered only when wealth is present
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates lasting and continual praise.
challenge.q: What does “for ever” imply about the poet’s praise?

paragraphs.idea: In contrast to the wicked man, the poet is like a green olive tree in the house of God. He trusts in God’s mercy forever, praises God because of what He has done, and waits on His good name before the saints.
